title: AI-Piloted F-16 Uses Sensor Data to Execute 27 Autonomous Combat Intercepts
excerpt: Lockheed Martin's Skunk Works demonstrated an AI agent using live infrared sensor feeds to autonomously fly the X-62A VISTA into tactical intercept positions against a T-38 jet across eight flight tests.
body:
• The X-62A VISTA, equipped with Lockheed Martin's Legion Pod infrared sensor, completed 27 AI-controlled intercepts against a live T-38 jet across eight flights at Edwards Air Force Base.
  • AI agents consumed classified infrared search and track data in real time, marking the first time onboard sensor feeds drove autonomous combat maneuvers on a fighter aircraft.
  • Skunk Works' "Supermassive" AI engine enabled full integration and ground testing in just three months, accelerating the path from simulation to live flight.
  • The milestone advances the U.S. Air Force's push toward collaborative combat aircraft and AI-augmented air dominance capabilities.

Lockheed Martin's Skunk Works division and the U.S. Air Force Test Pilot School have demonstrated an artificial intelligence agent using live sensor data to autonomously pilot a fighter jet into combat intercept positions, according to an announcement from the company on August 4, 2026.

The X-62A Variable In-flight Simulation Test Aircraft (VISTA), a modified F-16D based at Edwards Air Force Base in California, was equipped with the Lockheed Martin Legion Pod, an infrared search and track (IRST) system. Over eight flights, the AI agent used targeting information from the pod to track a live T-38 jet and execute 27 autonomous intercepts, with no pilot input on the flight controls during the maneuvers.

Closing the Sensor-to-Action Loop

The test series marked what Lockheed Martin described as a "closed-loop AI combat test," where the X-62 autonomously processed real-time sensor streams rather than relying on simulated target data. The AI agent consumed classified IRST feeds, identified the target aircraft, and maneuvered the fighter into a tactical intercept position without human intervention.

https://x.com/LockheedMartin/status/2084639964134801547

"Our autonomous agents consumed classified infrared search and track feeds and executed combat-critical maneuvers in real time. This achievement marks a decisive advance toward delivering AI-augmented air dominance for the United States."

— Ron Fehlen, Vice President and General Manager, Lockheed Martin Skunk Works

The distinction between simulated and real sensor data is critical. Previous AI flight tests on the X-62A, including within-visual-range dogfights under DARPA's Air Combat Evolution (ACE) program in 2023 and missile-evasion demonstrations under the Have Remy program in February 2026, relied on simulated threat cues. This latest campaign fed the AI agent data from an operational sensor in the same format pilots would encounter in actual combat scenarios.

Rapid Development Through Simulation

Skunk Works credited its "Supermassive" AI agent generation capability with dramatically compressing the development timeline. Full integration and ground testing of the AI agents with the X-62 occurred in just three months, according to the company. The Supermassive engine trains agents through billions of simulated engagements before transitioning them to high-fidelity simulators and then to live flight.

Stacy Kubicek, vice president and general manager of Lockheed Martin Sensors and Global Sustainment, said the test demonstrated how sensing and autonomous AI could function as "a force multiplier to make faster, more informed action in complex environments."

Building Toward Autonomous Combat Aircraft

The X-62A VISTA serves as the U.S. Air Force's primary testbed for autonomous flight technology, operated by the Air Force Test Pilot School's research division at Edwards. Since 2022, the aircraft has hosted AI agents from DARPA's ACE program and the Air Force Research Laboratory's Autonomous Air Combat Operations (AACO) initiative.

The platform is now undergoing a broader Mission Systems Upgrade funded by the Pentagon's Test Resource Management Center, which includes the addition of Raytheon's PhantomStrike active electronically scanned array radar. That upgrade, announced in December 2025, will allow AI agents to control radar sensors directly, processing raw data through machine learning in ways described as "inaccessible or unachievable by human use."

The work feeds directly into the Air Force's Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) program, which aims to field autonomous drone wingmen alongside crewed fighters. Three CCA prototypes from Anduril, General Atomics, and Northrop Grumman are in various stages of development and testing.

What's Next

Lockheed Martin said the proven framework from this experiment will enable the X-62 to demonstrate "seamless integration of combat systems, sensors and airborne AI agents within a next-generation mesh network" as part of the ongoing Mission Systems Upgrade. The company's engineers are working to advance technology roadmaps in coordination with operators to ensure what it calls "American leadership in AI and autonomy."

The achievement comes at a time when AI-enabled military systems are drawing increased attention from defense planners globally, with multiple nations investing in autonomous combat capabilities. For India, which has been developing its own autonomous aircraft programs and deepening defense technology cooperation with the United States, the rapid maturation of AI-driven combat systems underscores the accelerating pace of change in modern air warfare doctrine.
